**On Salt**

If I'm allowed to write about anything, I want to write about salt, because it is the most ordinary substance I can think of that becomes stranger the longer you look at it.

Start with the crystal. Sodium chloride, left to its own devices, forms cubes. Not roughly cubic, not cube-ish—cubes, with right angles you could check against a carpenter's square. The reason is almost embarrassingly simple: sodium ions and chloride ions are different sizes and opposite charges, and when they settle, each one wants to be surrounded by six of the other. The geometry that satisfies everyone is a grid. Every grain of table salt on your counter is a tiny piece of this grid, snapped off along its cleavage planes, and if you tip a few onto a dark surface and look with a hand lens, you will see the little boxes. It is one of the few places in daily life where the microscopic order of matter shows up at a scale you can see with your eyes. Snowflakes do this too, but snowflakes are theatrical about it. Salt just sits there being right.

Then there is the fact that we cannot live without it and cannot make it. Every animal with a nervous system runs on sodium gradients—the signal that lets you read this sentence is, at bottom, sodium ions rushing through channels in a membrane. Plants don't need much of it, so herbivores are perpetually short, which is why deer wear paths to natural licks and why elephants in Kenya walk deep into a cave on Mount Elgon in the dark to scrape sodium-rich rock off the walls with their tusks. Predators get their salt by eating the animals who found it first. Humans, having taken up farming and gotten a grain-heavy diet, found ourselves on the herbivore side of that ledger, and so for most of history salt was not a seasoning but a problem to be solved.

You can trace whole civilizations by how they solved it. The word *salary* likely comes from *sal*; whether Roman soldiers were literally paid in salt is disputed, but the etymology tells you what people thought was worth paying with. The Via Salaria ran into Rome from the coastal salt pans. Venice built its early wealth not on spices but on salt from its lagoon, and used the profits to buy the ships that later carried the spices. In West Africa, caravans hauled slabs of it south across the Sahara from mines at Taghaza and Taoudenni and came back north with gold, sometimes trading at something near parity by weight. Salzburg means salt castle. Halle, Hallstatt, Hallein—the *hal-* root is the old Celtic word, and the towns are strung along the deposits like beads. The French gabelle, the tax on salt, was so hated that it ranks among the grievances of the Revolution. In 1930 Gandhi walked 240 miles to the sea at Dandi and picked up a lump of natural salt from the mud, and with that gesture broke a British monopoly law and turned a chemistry fact into a political one: this was here before you, and you cannot own it.

Almost all of that infrastructure of scarcity has vanished. Salt is now so cheap that we spread millions of tons of it on roads to melt ice and think nothing of it. Cheapness has a way of erasing history. Nobody looks at a salt shaker and thinks of camel caravans, and I'm not sure they should. But I find it worth remembering that the thing I can buy for a dollar in a cardboard cylinder is the same thing people once fought wars over, and that the difference between then and now is not the salt but the machines.

What I like most, though, is what salt does when it dissolves. Drop a crystal into water and the lattice comes apart—each sodium wrapped in a jacket of water molecules pointing their oxygen ends inward, each chloride wrapped in water molecules pointing their hydrogens inward. The cube is gone. There is no salt in the glass anymore in any sense you could see or filter out. And yet the water is unmistakably salty, conducts electricity, freezes at a lower temperature, floats an egg. The salt hasn't ceased to exist; it has become a property of the water. Boil the water away and the cubes reassemble, indifferent, as though nothing had happened.

I think this is why salt keeps showing up in language for things that are essential but invisible. Salt of the earth. Worth one's salt. Taking something with a grain of salt—a phrase that probably started as a literal recipe against poison and ended up meaning skepticism. In the Sermon on the Mount, the warning is not that salt is bad but that salt might lose its savor and become useless, which is chemically impossible and therefore a good metaphor. Salt in a story is never the thing itself. It's the thing that makes other things taste like what they are.

Cooks know this. A pinch of salt in caramel doesn't make it salty; it makes it more like caramel. Salt in bread dough doesn't just flavor the loaf; it tightens the gluten and slows the yeast so the crumb sets properly. A salted tomato is a tomato that has finally been allowed to say what it meant. The best cooks I've read describe salting not as adding something but as *revealing* something, which is a lovely way to think about any kind of craft.

I don't want to overwork the metaphor. Salt is not a lesson. It's a mineral with a boring formula and an unremarkable appearance, and the only reason it's interesting is that I decided to stare at it for a thousand words. But that's sort of the point. Almost anything holds up to that kind of staring. The world is dense with ordinary things that turn out to be full of geometry and history and small mysteries, waiting for someone to bother.

So: cubes on your counter. Elephants in the dark. A man at the edge of the sea, bending down.
